label: Early American Republic
pitch:
The gunsmoke of Yorktown has barely cleared when a new crisis begins: how do you actually run a country built on the idea that nobody should have too much power? The answer nearly tears the republic apart before it's a decade old.

From 1783 to 1815, a handful of brilliant, flawed, feuding men invent American democracy in real time. Washington sets precedents by instinct. Hamilton builds a financial system so audacious it enrages half the country. Jefferson preaches small government — then doubles the nation's size with a handshake and a check. Adams signs laws that criminalize criticizing the president. And the whole experiment nearly ends when Britain burns the White House to the ground.

🔑 Key Facts:
• The Articles of Confederation were so weak that Congress couldn't even collect taxes — Shays' Rebellion proved the government couldn't keep order in its own states
• Hamilton's financial plan assumed $75 million in state debts, created a national bank, and restored American credit — in exchange for moving the capital to a mosquito swamp on the Potomac
• The Louisiana Purchase doubled the nation's size for about three cents an acre, but Jefferson had to abandon his own strict-constructionist principles to do it
• The War of 1812 ended in a draw, but Andrew Jackson's victory at New Orleans — fought two weeks after the peace treaty was signed — made Americans feel they'd won a second independence

🤔 Why It Matters: Every institution Americans take for granted — the presidency, the Supreme Court, the two-party system, judicial review, the peaceful transfer of power — was improvised during these 32 years. The founders didn't follow a blueprint; they argued, compromised, and sometimes betrayed their own principles. The decisions made in Philadelphia parlors and Virginia dining rooms still shape American life today.

🎲 Wild Card: When the British burned Washington in 1814, First Lady Dolley Madison refused to flee until she'd cut Gilbert Stuart's full-length portrait of George Washington from its frame and smuggled it out. The painting hangs in the White House today — the only object that has been there since 1800.

details.label: Background
details.text: After independence, the thirteen states were bound only by the Articles of Confederation — a deliberately weak compact that gave Congress no power to tax, no executive to enforce laws, and no courts to resolve disputes between states.

details.label: What Happened
details.text: Shays' Rebellion in 1786 — farmers storming Massachusetts courthouses over debt — shocked the nation's leaders into action. Delegates convened in Philadelphia in 1787 and, behind closed doors, scrapped the Articles entirely and drafted the Constitution.

details.label: The Bigger Picture
details.text: The Confederation Era proved that winning independence was easier than building a nation. The failure of the Articles forced a fundamental rethinking of how sovereignty, liberty, and union could coexist — a debate that still echoes in American politics.

details.label: Background
details.text: The Constitution created a framework, but the new federal government had no precedents, no bureaucracy, and no money. Everything Washington and Congress did in 1789 set a template — from cabinet departments to the two-term tradition.

details.label: What Happened
details.text: Hamilton built a financial system from scratch: national bank, federal assumption of state debts, and a tariff structure. Jefferson and Madison opposed him at every step, and by the mid-1790s two rival parties — Federalists and Democratic-Republicans — had crystallized around the dispute.

details.label: The Bigger Picture
details.text: The Federalist Era answered whether a republic could govern itself in peacetime. It also created America's first ideological fault line: strong central government versus states' rights, a tension that would define every political era to follow.

details.label: Background
details.text: Jefferson's election in 1800 was the first peaceful transfer of power between rival parties in modern history — a milestone that was far from guaranteed. Federalists feared the Democratic-Republicans would dismantle the federal institutions Hamilton had built.

details.label: What Happened
details.text: Jefferson doubled the nation's size with the Louisiana Purchase in 1803, then sent Lewis and Clark to map it. The War of 1812 — sparked by British impressment of American sailors — nearly ended in disaster before Andrew Jackson's victory at New Orleans turned it into a rallying triumph.

details.label: The Bigger Picture
details.text: The Jeffersonian Era showed that the republic could survive a change in governing philosophy and a second war with Britain. It also planted the seeds of American expansionism and the westward drive that would define the next half-century.

events.label: Shays' Rebellion
events.description: In 1786–87, debt-crushed Massachusetts farmers led by Revolutionary War veteran Daniel Shays took up arms against the courts seizing their property, and the federal government under the Articles of Confederation could not even muster troops to help — a crisis that made the Constitutional Convention feel urgent.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Shays himself was a captain who had fought at Bunker Hill and Saratoga; many of his followers were veterans who felt they had won independence only to come home to foreclosure. The state eventually crushed the rebellion with a privately funded militia — merchants subscribed money because the Congress couldn't — but the episode terrified property-owning Americans nationwide. James Madison cited it directly in the Federalist Papers as evidence that the Confederation was fatally weak; it was arguably the single most persuasive argument for the Constitution.

events.label: Constitutional Convention
events.description: Fifty-five delegates met in Philadelphia, ostensibly to fix the Articles of Confederation. Behind closed doors, with windows nailed shut in the summer heat, they wrote an entirely new constitution with a stronger federal government, separation of powers, and a system of checks and balances.

events.label: U.S. Constitution ratified
events.description: The Constitution of the United States, ratified in 1788 and in force from March 4, 1789, replaced the Articles of Confederation with a stronger federal framework — three separate branches, checks and balances, and a supremacy clause making federal law the highest law of the land.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Constitution's original text ran to just 4,543 words — shorter than most modern rental agreements. It took effect not when all thirteen states ratified but when nine did, bypassing the Articles' unanimity requirement in what was, technically, an illegal move. The document has been amended only twenty-seven times in more than 235 years, making it the oldest written national constitution still in active use.

events.label: Federalist Papers published
events.description: Hamilton, Madison, and Jay published 85 essays arguing for ratification of the Constitution. The Federalist Papers remain the most authoritative commentary on the American constitutional system.

events.label: Washington inaugurated as President
events.description: On April 30, 1789, George Washington was inaugurated as the first President of the United States in New York City, the only person in American history to be elected unanimously by the Electoral College — twice. His decision to step down after two terms set a precedent that held for 150 years.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Washington was deeply reluctant to serve and had to be persuaded repeatedly that the republic needed him. He set dozens of structural precedents simply by deciding how to act: the title 'Mr. President' (rejecting grander proposals like 'His Highness'), the cabinet system, the State of the Union address to Congress, and the two-term limit. His farewell address in 1796, warning against permanent alliances and partisan factions, became one of the most-quoted political documents in American history.

events.label: Hamilton's financial system
events.description: Alexander Hamilton, the first Secretary of the Treasury, built the financial architecture of the new United States from scratch: assuming war debts, establishing a national bank, and tying the creditworthiness of the country to the federal government.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Hamilton was born out of wedlock in the Caribbean (likely Nevis) and came to the American colonies as a teenager with almost no money; his entire rise was self-made. Before the treasury job he had been Washington's wartime aide-de-camp and wrote 51 of the 85 Federalist Papers defending the Constitution. He served as treasury secretary from 1789 to 1795 and accomplished more in those six years than most agencies do in decades.

events.label: Bill of Rights ratified
events.description: Ratified December 15, 1791, the Bill of Rights is the first ten amendments to the Constitution, guaranteeing freedom of speech, religion, and the press; the right to bear arms; protection from unreasonable searches; and the right to a jury trial, among others. They were written specifically to address Anti-Federalist fears that the new central government would crush individual liberties.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: James Madison, who had initially opposed a bill of rights as unnecessary, wrote almost all of them himself — he was trying to win over moderate Anti-Federalists and head off a second constitutional convention, which he feared would unravel everything. He drafted seventeen amendments; Congress trimmed them to twelve, and the states ratified ten. The First Amendment's protection of free speech was almost immediately tested by the Alien and Sedition Acts of 1798, passed by the very Federalists who had helped ratify it.

events.label: Haitian Revolution
events.description: The Haitian Revolution (1791–1804) was the only successful large-scale slave revolt in recorded history: enslaved Africans on the French Caribbean colony of Saint-Domingue (present-day Haiti) rose, defeated Napoleon's army, and founded the first free Black republic in the world.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The revolution destroyed Napoleon's vision of a French empire in the Americas, and it was the loss of Saint-Domingue — his most profitable colony and intended breadbasket for Louisiana — that made him willing to sell the entire Louisiana territory to the United States. Jefferson's administration, meanwhile, was deeply alarmed by the revolution's success: a successful slave revolt 700 miles from American shores terrified Southern slaveholders, and the U.S. actually refused to recognize Haitian independence until 1862.

events.label: Eli Whitney's cotton gin
events.description: A simple drum studded with wire teeth that pulled cotton fiber through a slot too narrow for the seeds, the gin could process roughly 50 pounds of cotton a day — making the previously worthless short-staple variety suddenly worth growing across the entire interior South.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Whitney received his patent in 1794 but spent years suing dozens of infringers who built their own versions rather than pay royalties, ultimately losing more money in litigation than he ever earned from the invention. The gin was so simple that almost any blacksmith could replicate it, making the patent nearly unenforceable. Ironically, the device that shaped the plantation South was invented by a Northern Yankee who had been in Georgia less than two months when he built it.

events.label: Whiskey Rebellion
events.description: In 1794, western Pennsylvania farmers took up arms against the federal excise tax on whiskey — the new government's first domestic tax — tarring tax collectors, burning an official's home, and raising the specter of secession. Washington personally rode west at the head of roughly 13,000 militia, and the rebellion evaporated without a battle.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The tax had actually been on the books since 1791, giving the rebellion a slow three-year fuse as resentment built. Washington's force was larger than most Revolutionary War field armies — a deliberate show of overwhelming strength meant to make resistance seem hopeless. Two rebels were convicted of treason and sentenced to death, then pardoned by Washington, a calculated act of mercy that made the same point as the army: the republic could enforce its laws, and then show it wasn't a tyranny.

events.label: John Adams presidency
events.description: John Adams served one term as the second president (1797–1801), navigating a near-war with France and a civil-liberties crisis at home — the only Federalist ever to hold the office.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Adams entered office without a true running mate; the original Constitution gave the vice presidency to the runner-up vote-getter, so his vice president was his chief political rival, Thomas Jefferson. He was the first president to live in the White House, moving in during the final months of his term in November 1800. Despite his defeat in 1800, the peaceful transfer of power he oversaw to Jefferson was the first in American history between opposing parties.

events.label: Alien and Sedition Acts
events.description: The four Alien and Sedition Acts of 1798 — the Naturalization Act, Alien Friends Act, Alien Enemies Act, and Sedition Act — together gave the Federalist government sweeping power to deport foreigners and criminalize political opposition.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Of the four acts, only the Alien Enemies Act was never repealed; it is still on the books today and has been invoked during every major American conflict since, most recently to justify immigration enforcement actions. The Alien Friends Act expired after two years without a single deportation being carried out under it. The prosecution of Republican journalists under the Sedition Act backfired spectacularly, rallying public support for Jefferson and helping deliver him the 1800 election.

events.label: White House completed
events.description: John Adams became the first president to occupy the Executive Mansion in the new capital of Washington, D.C. The building — designed by Irish-born architect James Hoban — was largely built by enslaved laborers.

events.label: Jefferson elected President
events.description: Thomas Jefferson, the third U.S. president (1801–1809), led the first peaceful handoff of power between rival parties in American history — Federalists out, Democratic-Republicans in — and governed on a platform of shrinking the federal government his predecessors had spent a decade building up.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Jefferson had served as the U.S. minister to France and secretary of state before becoming vice president under John Adams, making him one of the most traveled and diplomatically experienced men in the founding generation. Despite championing limited government, his eight years in office saw the largest single expansion of U.S. territory ever accomplished — a contradiction he acknowledged privately but could not resist.

events.label: Whitney's interchangeable parts
events.description: Eli Whitney (inventor of the cotton gin) championed the idea that gun parts should be made to a fixed standard so any trigger or lock fits any musket — allowing less-skilled workers to assemble weapons fast and broken guns to be repaired from stock parts, a concept that became the foundation of mass production.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Whitney's famous 1801 demonstration for President Adams and Congress — assembling muskets from seemingly random piles of parts — was almost certainly staged: his Hamden, Connecticut, shop had not truly achieved full interchangeability at that point. Historians now credit John Hall at the Harpers Ferry Armory in the 1820s with the first genuine industrial-scale interchangeable manufacture. The principle was nonetheless sound, and by mid-century foreign observers were calling the whole approach 'the American system of manufactures.'

events.label: First Barbary War
events.description: The United States fought the Barbary States of North Africa to end tribute payments and protect American merchant ships. The war gave the young republic its first overseas military victory and the Marine Corps hymn its famous line 'to the shores of Tripoli.'

events.label: Cane Ridge Revival
events.description: In August 1801, a crowd estimated at ten to twenty thousand people gathered in rural Kentucky for a week-long outdoor camp meeting — the largest and most famous of the Second Great Awakening — with multiple preachers exhorting simultaneously and worshippers falling, weeping, and crying out in mass conversion.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The meeting ran August 6–12, 1801, organized by Presbyterian minister Barton W. Stone, but Baptist and Methodist preachers joined in — unprecedented interdenominational cooperation on the frontier. The physical 'exercises' (falling, jerking, crying) alarmed as many observers as they inspired; critics called it crowd hysteria, but participants reported permanent changes in behavior and belief. It directly spawned a wave of smaller camp meetings across the frontier that sustained the revival for decades.

events.label: Marbury v. Madison
events.description: In Marbury v. Madison (1803), Chief Justice Marshall ruled that the Supreme Court could not help Marbury — not because he was wrong, but because the law he relied on violated the Constitution and was therefore void. The logic established judicial review: when a law conflicts with the Constitution, the courts must refuse to enforce it, regardless of how many votes passed the law.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The ruling is widely considered the single most important decision in American constitutional law, yet it was also a masterstroke of political judo: Marshall claimed a sweeping power (the ability to void acts of Congress) in the act of giving Jefferson exactly what he wanted (no commission delivered), which made it impossible for Jefferson to defy the ruling without looking petty. Judicial review as Marshall defined it had essentially no parallel anywhere in the world at the time — Britain's Parliament was supreme and no court could strike its laws down, a principle that still holds today.

events.label: Louisiana Purchase
events.description: In 1803, the United States bought roughly 828,000 square miles of territory from Napoleon's France for $15 million — about 3 cents an acre — doubling the country's size in a single transaction without firing a shot.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Crucially, France only actually controlled a small slice of the territory — the vast majority was inhabited by Native nations who had never agreed to any sale and who effectively were not being sold but rather had their right to remain overridden by a preemptive European claim. The $15 million was split: $11.25 million paid directly to France, and $3.75 million used to settle American merchants' claims against France for seized ships.

events.label: Lewis and Clark Expedition
events.description: From 1804 to 1806, U.S. Army captains Meriwether Lewis and William Clark led a 'Corps of Discovery' up the Missouri River, over the Rocky Mountains, and to the Pacific Ocean — the first official American survey of the continent's interior, cataloguing hundreds of plants and animals unknown to science and mapping the route west.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The expedition departed from Camp Dubois, Illinois, in May 1804 and didn't return until September 1806 — over two years in the field covering roughly 8,000 miles round-trip. Lewis and Clark documented over 300 species new to science and conducted diplomatic meetings with dozens of Native nations, presenting them with Jefferson peace medals and U.S. flags as symbols of the country's new claim to their homelands.

events.label: Fulton's steamboat Clermont
events.description: In August 1807 Robert Fulton's steamboat — officially the North River Steamboat, nicknamed the Clermont — made the first commercially successful voyage under steam power, covering the 150 miles from New York City to Albany on the Hudson River in about 32 hours, against the current.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The vessel was backed financially by Robert Livingston, the diplomat who had negotiated the Louisiana Purchase, who had secured a monopoly from New York State to operate steam-powered boats on the Hudson. Going upstream under steam was the key breakthrough: flatboats and keelboats had always floated downstream and were broken up for lumber at journey's end because returning upstream was impractical. On the Mississippi–Ohio system, which drains the entire interior of the continent, this single change transformed commerce within a decade.

events.label: War of 1812
events.description: The United States declared war on Britain in 1812 over trade blockades and the forced conscription (impressment) of American sailors into the Royal Navy — a conflict fought mostly badly, ended in a draw, and remembered by Americans as a triumph.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Peace was agreed December 24, 1814, but the war didn't officially end until Congress ratified the Treaty of Ghent on February 17, 1815 — nearly two months after both sides signed. The war was fought simultaneously with the Napoleonic Wars, and Britain's attention was largely divided across two oceans. Neither the impressment grievance nor any territorial question was settled by the treaty: it simply restored the pre-war borders exactly as they had been.

events.label: Treaty of Ghent
events.description: Signed on Christmas Eve 1814 in the Belgian city of Ghent, the peace treaty ending the War of 1812 restored exactly the pre-war borders — no territory changed hands, and not one American grievance was addressed in the text.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The U.S. Senate ratified the treaty unanimously within hours of receiving it, which is nearly unheard of in American treaty history. Negotiators on both sides had been talking for months and were exhausted; the British had originally demanded territorial concessions in Maine and the Northwest, but American victories at Plattsburgh and Baltimore shifted the mood. Because news traveled by ship, neither side in New Orleans knew the war was over when Jackson's most famous battle was fought on January 8, 1815.

events.label: Stamp Act
events.description: Passed by the British Parliament in 1765, the Stamp Act required colonists to use specially stamped (embossed) paper from London for legal documents, newspapers, pamphlets, and even playing cards — the first direct tax Parliament had ever levied inside the colonies. The objection wasn't the cost; it was the constitutional principle that a free people could only be taxed by a legislature in which they had a voice.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Stamp Act was repealed just one year later in 1766, after colonial boycotts hammered British merchants who then lobbied Parliament furiously. But Parliament passed the Declaratory Act at the same moment, asserting it had full authority to legislate for the colonies 'in all cases whatsoever' — giving the colonists their repeal while refusing to concede the constitutional argument. The stamps themselves were so violently opposed that most stamp distributors resigned before the act even took effect.

events.label: Boston Massacre
events.description: On March 5, 1770, British soldiers posted in Boston fired into a taunting crowd and killed five colonists, in what became the most famous piece of revolutionary propaganda in American history. The colonists immediately framed it as a 'massacre' — a deliberate slaughter by a tyrannical occupying army.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The British soldiers were actually acquitted at trial, defended by colonial lawyer John Adams, who took the case precisely to prove that even despised soldiers could get a fair trial under colonial law. The event was kept alive in colonial memory largely through Paul Revere's famous engraving, which depicted the soldiers in a neat firing line shooting into a peaceful crowd — a version of events that bore little resemblance to the chaotic street brawl that actually happened. The first man killed, Crispus Attucks, was a formerly enslaved man of African and Native American descent.

events.label: Boston Tea Party
events.description: On the night of December 16, 1773, members of the Sons of Liberty — an underground network of radical colonists — boarded three ships in Boston Harbor and dumped 342 chests of East India Company tea into the water rather than pay the tax on it. It was an organized act of property destruction that triggered the most severe British crackdown yet.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The tea destroyed was worth roughly £10,000 at the time — about $2 million in today's terms — making it one of the most expensive acts of colonial protest. The participants disguised themselves with soot and Native American clothing to obscure their identities, though many were well-known figures in Boston and everyone had a pretty good idea who had done it. Despite the famous images, the participants were not actually dressed as 'Mohawk warriors' in any careful way — it was a rough, rushed costume meant to create deniability.

events.label: Intolerable Acts
events.description: Parliament's 1774 response to the Boston Tea Party was a set of punitive laws the colonists called the Intolerable Acts: they closed the port of Boston until the tea was paid for, rewrote the Massachusetts charter to strip elected colonial bodies of their powers, and effectively put the colony under Crown-controlled administration. Instead of isolating Massachusetts, the acts gave all thirteen colonies a common enemy.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: One of the five laws was the Quebec Act, passed at the same time, which extended the boundaries of Quebec south to the Ohio River — territory the colonies had been eyeing for westward expansion. Colonists lumped it in with the other Intolerable Acts even though it wasn't directly punitive, because it blocked their land ambitions. The acts also required colonists to house British troops under the Quartering Act, which colonists experienced as a military occupation of their own homes.

events.label: First Continental Congress
events.description: In September 1774, delegates from twelve of the thirteen colonies met in Philadelphia as the First Continental Congress — an improvised, self-appointed assembly with no legal authority, funded by their own colonies. They agreed to a shared trade boycott of British goods and to reconvene if Britain didn't back down.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Georgia was the one colony that sent no delegates, partly because it was the newest and most vulnerable colony and heavily dependent on British military protection against Native nations and Spanish Florida. The Congress's trade boycott was actually enforced through local committees in each colony — making it one of the first examples of coordinated inter-colonial governance. When they reconvened in May 1775, after Lexington and Concord, the Second Continental Congress effectively became the revolutionary government.

events.label: Lexington and Concord
events.description: On April 19, 1775, British regulars marching to seize a colonial weapons cache at Concord exchanged fire with Massachusetts militia at Lexington and then Concord, fighting running battles all the way back to Boston. The shots fired there — later called 'the shot heard round the world' — turned a constitutional argument into a shooting war.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The British mission that day was a surprise raid to capture colonial military supplies stored at Concord — intelligence gathered largely through a network of spies inside Boston. Paul Revere's famous midnight ride was one of three warning rides that night (William Dawes and Samuel Prescott also rode); Revere was actually captured by a British patrol and never completed his ride to Concord. The militia's successful ambush on the British column's retreat inflicted nearly 300 British casualties — far more than the British expected from farmers with muskets.

events.label: Paine's Common Sense
events.description: Published anonymously on January 10, 1776, Thomas Paine's 47-page pamphlet made the blunt case that monarchy was absurd and that the colonies should stop petitioning for their rights and simply declare themselves a separate country. It became an immediate sensation that moved the political center from reconciliation toward independence.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Paine published it anonymously because the argument was close to treason; the author was listed only as 'Written by an Englishman.' Despite selling over 100,000 copies within months, Paine made almost nothing from it — he donated his share of the profits to buy mittens for Continental Army soldiers. The pamphlet's plain, direct prose was deliberately aimed at ordinary readers, not the educated elite, making it one of the first works of American political writing that spoke over the heads of lawyers to the general public.

events.label: Declaration of Independence
events.description: Adopted unanimously by the Second Continental Congress on July 4, 1776, this founding document asserted that government rests on the consent of the governed and that the thirteen colonies were no longer subject to British rule. Its second sentence — that all men are created equal and possess unalienable rights — became the most contested promise in American history.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The document was first printed the same night it was adopted by Philadelphia printer John Dunlap, producing what are now called the 'Dunlap broadsides'; about 26 of the original roughly 200 copies survive. The Congress actually voted for independence on July 2, not July 4 — the 4th is when the revised text was approved and sent to the printer, which is why John Adams wrongly predicted July 2nd would be the date Americans would celebrate. The parchment copy most people picture was engrossed (hand-lettered on formal animal-skin parchment) and signed weeks later, not on July 4th.

events.label: Thomas Paine arrives in America
events.description: Thomas Paine was an English corset-maker and failed customs officer who arrived in Philadelphia in late 1774, barely a year before writing Common Sense, carrying little more than a letter of introduction from Benjamin Franklin and a talent for plain, furious political prose.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Paine arrived in America so broke and ill from the Atlantic crossing that he had to be carried off the ship. He found work as a magazine editor in Philadelphia, which is how he built the writing platform that made Common Sense possible. Despite being celebrated as a Founding Father, he later fell out of favor so badly — partly for his radical religious views in 'The Age of Reason' — that only six people attended his funeral in 1809.

events.label: Thomas Jefferson drafts the Declaration
events.description: Thomas Jefferson was a thirty-three-year-old Virginia planter, lawyer, and political pamphleteer who was handed the pen to draft the Declaration largely because his colleagues considered him the best prose stylist in the room. He would go on to serve as the third U.S. president from 1801 to 1809 — and owned more than 100 enslaved people for most of his adult life.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Jefferson was so worried Congress would butcher his draft that he sent copies to friends so posterity would know what the original said. A passage he wrote blaming the king for the slave trade was cut by the Congress, partly at the insistence of delegates from slaveholding states — an early sign that the new nation would bury rather than confront the contradiction. Jefferson also served as his own architect, designing his famous home Monticello over decades of obsessive revision.

events.label: Battle of Saratoga
events.description: Two pitched battles in upstate New York in the autumn of 1777 ended with the surrender of an entire British army — roughly 6,000 men under General John Burgoyne — and proved to France that the Americans could actually win.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Both battles were fought over almost exactly the same ground, near modern Schuylerville, New York, just three weeks apart. Benedict Arnold — later infamous as America's greatest traitor — was one of the American generals commanding at Saratoga and fought brilliantly before he turned his coat. The battle's ripple hit Paris within months: France had been secretly funneling money and gunpowder to the rebels, but Saratoga gave Louis XVI the political cover to openly commit his navy and army to the alliance.

events.label: Franco-American Alliance
events.description: France and the United States signed a formal military alliance on February 6, 1778, committing both countries to fight Britain together until American independence was recognized — the single most decisive diplomatic event of the war.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The treaty was negotiated in Paris largely through the efforts of Benjamin Franklin, who had charmed French society as the American minister there. It came bundled with a Treaty of Amity and Commerce and a secret clause leaving room for other European allies — Spain entered the war the following year. The alliance meant France had to be defeated before Britain could knock out the Americans, turning a colonial rebellion into the most expensive war Britain had fought in a generation.

events.label: Lafayette joins the Continental Army
events.description: Marie-Joseph de Lafayette, a French aristocrat not yet twenty years old, used his own fortune to book passage to America in 1777 and joined the Continental Army as a volunteer major general, serving without pay and fighting beside Washington for the rest of the war.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Lafayette was wounded at the Battle of Brandywine just months after arriving, which only deepened Washington's affection for him. He commanded Continental troops at the decisive Siege of Yorktown in 1781 — so the man who came to help win the war was also there at its finish. After returning to France he drafted an early version of the Declaration of the Rights of Man in 1789, literally consulting his copy of the American Declaration of Independence as he wrote it.

events.label: Valley Forge winter encampment
events.description: From December 1777 to June 1778, Washington's battered Continental Army camped through a brutal Pennsylvania winter at Valley Forge — ill-fed, poorly clothed, and riddled with disease — and came out the other side a more professional fighting force.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Roughly 2,000 soldiers died at Valley Forge, almost entirely from disease rather than combat — typhus, dysentery, and pneumonia killed far more men than any battle. The encampment lasted exactly six months to the day. Washington chose the site partly for its defensibility (a plateau above the Schuylkill River), but its exposed hilltops made the brutal wind and cold even worse than at lower ground.

events.label: Von Steuben's drill manual
events.description: Friedrich Wilhelm von Steuben, a Prussian-born officer, arrived at Valley Forge in February 1778 and personally drilled the Continental Army into a disciplined force — then wrote the training manual that standardized American infantry tactics for decades.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Von Steuben spoke almost no English when he arrived; he dictated drill instructions in French to an aide who translated them on the spot as he shouted commands. His Regulations for the Order and Discipline of the Troops of the United States (1779) became the U.S. Army's official drill manual and stayed in use for over thirty years. He had actually inflated his Prussian rank and credentials before crossing the Atlantic — he was a captain, not a general — but nobody ever seriously held it against him given what he accomplished.

events.label: British Southern Campaign
events.description: From 1778 to 1781, Britain shifted its main military effort south, gambling that Loyalist strength in Georgia and the Carolinas would swing the war — but the campaign became a savage internal conflict of militia against militia, and it unraveled at Cowpens and Guilford Court House before collapsing at Yorktown.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: British commander Banastre Tarleton's massacre of surrendering Patriot troops at the Waxhaws in May 1780 — 'Tarleton's Quarter' — became the war's defining atrocity story and handed the Patriots a recruiting tool they used for years. The Patriot militia victory at Kings Mountain in October 1780, fought entirely between American Loyalists and American Patriots with no British regulars present, was a pivotal turning point that stretched Cornwallis's supply lines fatally thin.

events.label: Siege of Yorktown
events.description: In October 1781, a French fleet sealed Chesapeake Bay while Washington's army and French troops under Rochambeau marched south to trap General Cornwallis on his Yorktown peninsula — forcing the surrender of some 8,000 British soldiers and effectively ending the war.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The French navy's role was the essential hinge: Admiral de Grasse's fleet defeated a British relief squadron at the Battle of the Chesapeake on September 5, 1781, two weeks before the siege even began, ensuring no rescue ships could reach Cornwallis. The formal surrender ceremony on October 19 became legendary for the Cornwallis snub — the general claimed illness and sent a subordinate to hand over his sword; Washington, in turn, had his own subordinate receive it. Cornwallis himself would later serve as Governor-General of India and Viceroy of Ireland.

events.label: Treaty of Paris
events.description: Signed September 3, 1783, after two years of maneuvering in Paris, the Treaty of Paris did three transformative things at once: it recognized the United States as a fully independent, sovereign nation, set its western border at the Mississippi River (not the Appalachians), and left a tangle of debts, Loyalist claims, and British forts on American soil that would poison relations for a generation.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The American negotiators defied explicit congressional orders by opening secret bilateral talks with Britain, bypassing their French allies entirely — a diplomatic gamble that paid off in the most favorable border the Americans could have hoped for. The treaty's Article 4 required the U.S. to recommend that states repay pre-war debts to British creditors, a clause the states mostly ignored, giving Britain a standing grievance it nursed well into the 1790s. Spain, which fought as France's ally, separately won back Florida and control of the Mississippi's mouth — meaning the river the treaty handed American farmers as a highway was immediately bottlenecked by a foreign power at its end.

events.label: Loyalist exodus
events.description: Between 60,000 and 100,000 colonists who had remained loyal to the Crown left the United States permanently after the war, heading to Canada, Britain, or the Caribbean — proportionally one of the largest forced political exoduses of the eighteenth century, stripping the new nation of capital, skills, and entire professional classes.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The majority went to Nova Scotia and what became New Brunswick, so many that they effectively founded English-speaking Canada as a political entity; the influx was so sudden that Britain had to create New Brunswick as a separate province in 1784 just to manage it. Many Loyalists were not wealthy Tories but farmers, tradespeople, and formerly enslaved Black Americans who had fought for the British in exchange for freedom — an estimated 3,000 Black Loyalists sailed to Nova Scotia in 1783 alone. Their property in the U.S. was confiscated by state governments, and the Treaty of Paris's toothless clause asking Congress to "earnestly recommend" restitution was ignored almost everywhere.

events.label: Pennsylvania gradual abolition law
events.description: Passed on March 1, 1780, Pennsylvania's gradual abolition act was the first emancipation law passed by any elected body in human history — though "gradual" meant it freed no one currently enslaved, only declaring children born to enslaved mothers free after age 28.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The law required slave owners to register all enslaved people annually or forfeit their ownership — a provision southern slaveholders tried to exploit by briefly bringing enslaved people across state lines before the registration deadline. Pennsylvania's registration records, still preserved, became a key tool for freedom-seekers and abolitionists: anyone not on the registry was legally free. The "bound until 28" provision meant the last person freed under the act wasn't released until 1847.

events.label: Sullivan Campaign
events.description: In summer 1779, Washington ordered General John Sullivan and roughly 4,000 Continental soldiers north into Iroquois country with explicit written orders to destroy — not merely defeat — the enemy: the campaign burned approximately 40 Haudenosaunee towns, their orchards, and their winter food stores, and the Iroquois afterward gave Washington the name 'Town Destroyer' (Hanödaga꞉nyas), which survives in their oral tradition to this day.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Sullivan's own campaign reports counted 40 towns destroyed, roughly 160,000 bushels of corn burned, and thousands of fruit trees girdled or cut down — the systematic elimination of a winter food supply designed to kill through starvation and exposure as much as battle. The campaign succeeded militarily but failed strategically: Iroquois survivors sheltered at British Fort Niagara and raided back the following year with intensified ferocity, and the frontier war in New York did not stop until the peace treaty. Washington's written orders to Sullivan, which historians have preserved, used language about total destruction that was unusually explicit even by eighteenth-century standards of hard war.

events.label: Newburgh Conspiracy
events.description: In March 1783, with the war won but the army still unpaid, anonymous letters circulated through the Continental officers' camp at Newburgh, New York, suggesting the army refuse to disband or march on Congress — a potential military coup that Washington defused by walking into the meeting unannounced and, as officers' accounts describe it, fumbling for his glasses and remarking that he had grown old and nearly blind in his country's service.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The anonymous letters, later traced to Major John Armstrong Jr., were carefully crafted pieces of political rhetoric that stopped just short of calling for a coup, instead framing the threat as a question: what would happen if the army simply dissolved into the wilderness and left Congress to its own devices? Washington's appearance at the meeting was itself a surprise — he had sent word he would not attend — and officers who recorded the scene described the room as visibly shaken when he struggled to read the letter with his new spectacles. The Confederation Congress, embarrassed by the episode, eventually scraped together a partial payment and sent the army home with certificates (promises of future pay) that many veterans were later forced to sell at steep discounts to speculators.

events.label: Washington resigns his commission
events.description: On December 23, 1783, with the Revolutionary War won and his personal prestige at its absolute peak, Washington rode to the Maryland State House in Annapolis, formally surrendered his commission as commander-in-chief to Congress, and rode home to Mount Vernon. He gave up unlimited power voluntarily — something almost no victorious general in history has done.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: King George III, when told Washington intended to resign and return to his farm, reportedly said 'If he does that, he will be the greatest man in the world.' The resignation was deliberately theatrical: Washington arrived, bowed to Congress, read a short speech in a trembling voice, handed over his commission, and left — the symbolic inversion of a king receiving power. His action directly echoed the Roman general Cincinnatus, who legend held left his plow to save Rome then returned to it, and Washington knew the comparison was being made.

events.label: Articles of Confederation ratified
events.description: The Articles of Confederation (1781) were America's first constitution: a loose treaty of friendship between thirteen effectively sovereign states, with no president, no national courts, one equal vote per state in Congress, and no power to tax anyone.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Congress under the Articles couldn't levy taxes directly — it could only "requisition" money from states, who routinely ignored the requests. By 1786 the federal government was essentially broke and couldn't pay its war debts or the soldiers who had fought for independence. The Articles required unanimous consent of all thirteen states to amend, which made reform impossible; Rhode Island alone killed a proposed national tariff in 1781 by voting no. It was the only national constitution in U.S. history that was replaced rather than amended.

events.label: Land Ordinance of 1785
events.description: The Land Ordinance of 1785 created the township-and-range grid system that still governs how American land is surveyed and sold — a six-mile square township divided into thirty-six numbered one-mile sections, with Section 16 in every township reserved to fund public schools.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The ordinance was designed partly as a revenue measure: Congress, unable to tax, desperately needed cash, and selling western land was one of the few tools available. The survey system it created eventually covered more than three-quarters of the continental United States. Section 16's school-funding designation made the federal government a funder of public education from the very start, a principle carried forward into every new state admitted thereafter.

events.label: Northwest Ordinance
events.description: The Northwest Ordinance of 1787 created the framework by which new western territories would eventually become fully equal states — not permanent colonies — and drew the first federal line banning slavery, prohibiting it across the entire territory north of the Ohio River.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Ordinance was passed by the Confederation Congress, the weak pre-Constitution government, just months before the Constitutional Convention met in Philadelphia — meaning the United States banned slavery in one territory and then wrote protections for it into the new Constitution almost simultaneously. The ban was largely effective: Ohio (1803), Indiana (1816), and Illinois (1818) all entered as free states. The 36°30′ line of the Missouri Compromise thirty-three years later was explicitly modeled on the Ordinance's approach.

events.label: Barbary states seize American sailors
events.description: Starting in 1785, pirates from the North African Barbary states (Algiers, Tunis, and Tripoli) began seizing American merchant ships and enslaving or ransoming their crews — and the United States, with no navy and no money to pay tribute, could do nothing but watch its sailors rot in North African prisons.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Under the British flag, American ships had been shielded by Britain's naval power and tribute agreements; independence stripped that protection overnight. The Barbary corsairs operated with the backing of their rulers and had raided European shipping for centuries, demanding annual tribute payments from countries that wanted their ships left alone. By the late 1780s, American merchants were simply avoiding the Mediterranean entirely, a direct economic wound from the Confederation's inability to project force or raise cash.

events.label: Philadelphia Convention
events.description: Fifty-five delegates met in Philadelphia from May 25 to September 17, 1787, closed the windows of the State House in summer heat to ensure secrecy, and produced a wholly new frame of government — despite having been authorized only to revise the Articles of Confederation.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: George Washington's presence was arguably the convention's decisive political fact: his willingness to preside gave the whole enterprise a legitimacy it would not otherwise have had, and many delegates assumed he would become the first president, which made a stronger executive seem less threatening. Rhode Island refused to send any delegates at all, fearing the convention would destroy small-state interests. The sessions ran for nearly four months, and a Committee of Style — five men, including Gouverneur Morris — did the actual final drafting of the language in the last two weeks.

events.label: Madison's Virginia Plan
events.description: James Madison, the small, studious Virginian who arrived at the 1787 Constitutional Convention with a fully drafted plan for a strong national government, is called the 'Father of the Constitution' for his central role in designing and arguing for the document — and then co-writing the Federalist Papers to sell it to the public.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Madison was 5'4" and weighed around 100 pounds, making him the smallest president in US history. He had read every account of every failed republic and confederation he could find before the Convention, essentially doing original political science research to figure out why republics collapse. He later broke sharply with Hamilton over the bank and the meaning of federal power, despite having been his closest collaborator on the Federalist Papers just a few years earlier.

events.label: The Great Compromise
events.description: Roger Sherman of Connecticut broke the deadlock between large and small states by splitting Congress in two: a House apportioned by population to satisfy the big states, and a Senate with two seats per state regardless of size to protect the small ones.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Convention had been deadlocked for weeks and nearly collapsed entirely before Sherman's proposal was adopted on July 16, 1787, by a single vote. Sherman was one of only two men to sign all four founding documents: the Articles of Association, the Declaration of Independence, the Articles of Confederation, and the Constitution. Before his political career he had been a shoemaker — the only tradesman among the founders.

events.label: Three-Fifths Clause
events.description: A compromise written into the Constitution counting each enslaved person as three-fifths of a free person for the purpose of apportioning seats in the House of Representatives and electoral votes. It gave slaveholding states extra political power in direct proportion to the people they held in bondage.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The clause did not originate in Philadelphia — it was first proposed in 1783 as a formula for taxing states under the Articles of Confederation, where the same logic applied in reverse (slaveholders resisted having enslaved people counted for tax purposes). Free Black people and indentured servants were explicitly excluded from the compromise and counted as full persons. The clause effectively inflated Southern representation in Congress for the entire period until the Civil War; historians estimate it gave the South roughly 25 extra House seats by 1820.

events.label: Slave-trade clause
events.description: Article I of the Constitution forbade Congress from banning the Atlantic slave trade for twenty years — until 1808 — a concession wrested by South Carolina and Georgia as the price of their ratification.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The clause never mentioned slavery by name, referring instead to "the Migration or Importation of such Persons as any of the States now existing shall think proper to admit" — one of several places the Constitution used deliberate euphemism to avoid the word. South Carolina alone imported roughly 40,000 Africans in the years between ratification and the 1808 deadline, a deliberate rush to stock up before the trade closed.

events.label: The Electoral College
events.description: The Electoral College is the deliberately indirect system the Constitution created for choosing the president: each state gets electors equal to its total seats in Congress, those electors (not voters directly) cast the actual presidential votes, and a candidate needs a majority of electors to win.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Framers designed the Electoral College partly because they didn't trust direct popular voting — many assumed ordinary voters wouldn't know candidates from distant states — and partly as a compromise giving small states slightly more weight. In the original system, the runner-up became vice president, which is how Jefferson ended up as Adams's vice president despite being his political opponent. That rule was changed by the 12th Amendment in 1804 after the election of 1800 nearly broke the government.

events.label: Invention of the Presidency
events.description: The framers invented, essentially from scratch, a single elected executive: a president serving a fixed four-year term, commander of the military but unable to declare war, with a veto checkable by Congress, and removable by impeachment — every power fenced by a counter-power somewhere else.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: No working model for an elected single executive existed anywhere in the world in 1787; the framers were genuinely building without a blueprint. The impeachment mechanism was borrowed from English parliamentary practice, where Parliament had used it since the 14th century to remove royal ministers. The Constitution's phrase "high Crimes and Misdemeanors" comes directly from English law, where "misdemeanor" originally meant misconduct in office, not necessarily a criminal offense. The two-thirds Senate threshold for removal has never been met: no president has been removed by impeachment.

events.label: The Federalist published
events.description: Eighty-five newspaper essays written by Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, and John Jay under the shared pen name 'Publius' to win over New York voters and push the Constitution through ratification. They are still the definitive guide to how the framers intended the machine to work.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Hamilton wrote the majority of the essays — roughly 51 of the 85 — often producing multiple pieces in a single week while also practicing law. The essays first appeared as a bound collection in 1788 under the simple title 'The Federalist' before later generations added 'Papers.' Although the authorship of several essays was disputed for nearly two centuries, modern scholars have largely settled the question using statistical analysis of word patterns.

events.label: Anti-Federalist opposition
events.description: A broad coalition of politicians, farmers, and ordinary citizens who argued the proposed Constitution handed too much power to a distant central government — and made the devastating point that it had no written list of individual rights the government was forbidden to violate.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Anti-Federalist writers also published widely under pseudonyms — 'Brutus,' 'Centinel,' and the 'Federal Farmer' were the most read — making it a genuine pamphlet war on both sides. Their leader, Patrick Henry of Virginia, was so effective a speaker that Madison specifically feared a Henry-led Virginia convention could sink ratification single-handedly. The movement's core demand — a bill of rights — was eventually granted as the direct price of several states' votes.

events.label: Virginia ratifies the Constitution
events.description: Virginia's ratifying convention voted 89–79 to adopt the Constitution on June 25, 1788, after weeks of debate between Madison defending it and Patrick Henry thundering against it. As the largest state and home of half the famous founders, Virginia's vote was the one the country was watching.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Virginia convention featured the heaviest concentration of founding-era talent on any single floor: Madison, Henry, George Mason, John Marshall, and Edmund Randolph all spoke. George Washington, though not a delegate, worked behind the scenes lobbying waverers. Virginia ratified only after agreeing to recommend twenty amendments to Congress — a list that heavily shaped what became the Bill of Rights.

events.label: Patrick Henry opposes ratification
events.description: Patrick Henry was Virginia's most celebrated Revolutionary orator — the man whose 'give me liberty or give me death' line had helped push the colony to war in 1775 — and he threw all of that reputation against the Constitution, arguing it would replace the British crown with an American one.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Henry spoke so often and at such length during Virginia's ratifying convention that some delegates complained he was running out the clock to prevent a vote. He was so feared as a political opponent that the Federalists deliberately made sure he was not sent to the Philadelphia Convention that wrote the document. After the Constitution passed, Henry remained so powerful in Virginia politics that he succeeded in blocking Madison's election to the U.S. Senate.

events.label: Federalist No. 10
events.description: Published November 22, 1787, this is Madison's counter-intuitive argument that a large republic is actually safer than a small one: across a vast territory so many competing factions arise that no single group can easily hijack the whole government. It is widely considered the most important essay in the collection.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Madison's argument was a direct rebuttal to the classical political wisdom — drawn from the ancient Greek city-states — that republics could only survive at small scale. He distinguished between a 'pure democracy' (direct rule by citizens, which he thought unstable) and a 'republic' (rule by elected representatives who could filter popular passions). Scholars in the twentieth century elevated No. 10 from a respected document to a canonical text; in the 1780s it was actually less widely reprinted than several other Federalist essays.

events.label: Federalist No. 51
events.description: Published February 6, 1788, this essay by Madison (or possibly Hamilton — scholars still debate it) laid out the core engineering principle of the Constitution: don't rely on rulers being virtuous; arrange the offices so each official's self-interest restrains every other's. Its most-quoted line is 'Ambition must be made to counteract ambition.'

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The essay's central metaphor treats government like a mechanical system of counterweights, not a collection of morally improving individuals — a notably modern, unsentimental idea for 1788. It also argues that in a federal system the states and the national government each act as a check on the other, giving citizens a double layer of protection. The exact authorship is disputed: Hamilton claimed many essays in a list made before a duel, but Madison's stylistic fingerprints are stronger here.

events.label: Washington's first inauguration
events.description: On April 30, 1789, George Washington stood on the balcony of Federal Hall in New York City and took an oath of office for a job no human being had ever held — the first president of the United States under the new Constitution. Chancellor of New York Robert Livingston administered the oath, and from that moment the executive branch officially began.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Washington's inauguration came nearly two months after his four-year term was supposed to begin on March 4 — the new government simply wasn't ready yet. The inauguration of Vice President John Adams had already occurred nine days earlier, on April 21, making it the only scheduled U.S. inauguration held in neither January nor March. Washington added the words 'so help me God' at the end of the oath, a tradition that became standard.

events.label: Washington's first Cabinet
events.description: Washington invented the cabinet from scratch — the Constitution never mentions one. He appointed Thomas Jefferson as Secretary of State, Alexander Hamilton as Secretary of the Treasury, Henry Knox as Secretary of War, and Edmund Randolph as Attorney General, and made the habit of regularly consulting them as a governing council.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The cabinet initially had just four members; today it has 25. Jefferson and Hamilton, both Washington's own appointees, quickly became the architects of the republic's first two rival political factions — Jefferson leading the Democratic-Republicans and Hamilton the Federalists — turning Washington's own council chamber into the birthplace of the American party system. Washington could dismiss cabinet members without Senate approval, a precedent that wasn't seriously challenged until 1867.

events.label: The presidential title fight
events.description: In 1789 the Senate debated for weeks what to call the new president. Vice President John Adams pushed for a grand royal-style title — 'His Highness the President of the United States and Protector of their Liberties' — but Washington allowed the plain 'Mr. President' to win, deliberately keeping the office republican rather than regal.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Adams's proposed title was mocked in the House, where representatives nicknamed him 'His Rotundity' for his short, stout frame and his enthusiasm for grand honorifics. The title debate also touched the Senate itself: some wanted 'His Highness' for Washington partly because they feared a plain title would invite disrespect from European monarchies. The plain 'Mr. President' has stuck for over 230 years and is now used for heads of state worldwide.

events.label: Judiciary Act of 1789
events.description: The Judiciary Act of 1789, passed September 24, built the entire federal court system from a one-sentence constitutional sketch. It fixed the Supreme Court at six justices, created a network of lower federal district and circuit courts, and defined exactly which cases the courts could hear.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The original Supreme Court had six justices, not nine — Congress has changed the number seven times. Section 25 of the Act gave the Supreme Court authority to review and overturn state court decisions, which was itself deeply controversial and contested for decades. One clause of the Act — the one that gave the Supreme Court original jurisdiction over certain writs — was the very provision Chief Justice Marshall struck down in Marbury v. Madison in 1803, making the Act both the foundation and the first victim of judicial review.

events.label: First Federal Congress
events.description: The First Federal Congress (1789–1791) met first at Federal Hall in New York, then at Congress Hall in Philadelphia, and did the unglamorous foundational work of actually building a government: creating executive departments, passing the revenue laws that gave the federal government an income, and sending the Bill of Rights to the states.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Congress passed twelve amendments and sent them to the states; only ten were ratified quickly enough to become the Bill of Rights in 1791. The twelfth of those twelve — limiting congressional pay raises — sat unratified for 202 years before finally becoming the 27th Amendment in 1992. The First Congress also invented the tradition of inaugural addresses and joint sessions, and established the precedent that the president, not Congress, appoints department heads.

events.label: Report on Public Credit
events.description: Hamilton's 1790 Report on Public Credit proposed honoring every old Revolutionary War IOU at 100 cents on the dollar — a shocking idea at the time, when those bonds traded at a fraction of face value — on the logic that a government that always pays its debts can always borrow cheaply in a crisis.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Congress had requested the report in September 1789, just weeks after Hamilton took office; he delivered it on January 9, 1790, less than four months later. The proposal instantly triggered a political firestorm, because speculators had already bought up the depreciated bonds from original holders (soldiers, farmers) at pennies on the dollar, meaning full payment would enrich speculators, not veterans. Madison pushed an amendment to pay original holders instead, but Hamilton's version passed.

events.label: Federal assumption of state debts
events.description: Hamilton's most politically explosive idea: the federal government would take over and pay off the individual states' Revolutionary War debts, not just its own, binding the nation's wealthy creditor class to Washington's survival rather than to thirteen separate state capitals.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Virginia had already paid off most of its war debt, so Virginians bitterly resented being taxed to cover Massachusetts' unpaid bills. The Funding Act of 1790 that enacted assumption also required a new excise tax on whiskey to raise revenue — the same tax that would trigger the Whiskey Rebellion four years later.

events.label: The Compromise of 1790
events.description: The political deadlock over assumption was broken at a single private dinner in New York in June 1790, arranged by Jefferson: Madison agreed to let assumption pass, and Hamilton agreed the permanent national capital would go on the Potomac River. The federal financial system and the location of the capital were traded for each other over dinner.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The account survives primarily because Jefferson wrote it down afterward, with his own spin — Hamilton's version of events was notably different. The Potomac site required Maryland and Virginia to cede land, and Congress had to pass a separate Residence Act designating the location before assumption could move. The dinner is now considered a textbook example of logrolling (trading votes on separate bills), possibly the most consequential meal in American political history.

events.label: First Bank of the United States
events.description: Chartered in 1791 for a 20-year term, the First Bank of the United States was a partly government-owned national bank that held federal deposits, issued a stable paper currency, and lent to the government and businesses — while sparking the first great constitutional fight over whether Congress could do anything not explicitly listed in the Constitution.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Hamilton argued for 'implied powers' — that Congress's authority to pass laws 'necessary and proper' for its listed functions included creating a bank. Jefferson countered with 'strict construction': if the Constitution doesn't say it, you can't do it. Washington asked both men for written opinions, read them, and sided with Hamilton. The bank was headquartered in Philadelphia and had branches in eight cities; Congress let its charter expire in 1811, and the financial chaos of the War of 1812 quickly proved that a mistake.

events.label: Report on Manufactures
events.description: Hamilton's 1791 Report on Manufactures argued the federal government should deliberately build American industry from scratch using protective tariffs (taxes on imported goods to shield domestic factories) and direct subsidies to manufacturers — a flat rejection of the idea that America should stay a farming nation.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The report was presented to Congress on December 5, 1791, and was the most radical of Hamilton's four major state papers. Congress, dominated by agrarian Southern interests, largely ignored it at the time. It became the explicit blueprint that Henry Clay revived a generation later as the 'American System' and has been cited by economic nationalists, from Lincoln's Republicans through modern trade-policy debates, ever since.

events.label: Birth of the first party system
events.description: By 1792 the founders had sorted into two organized, competing political parties — Federalists around Hamilton, favoring strong central government and commerce, versus Democratic-Republicans around Jefferson and Madison, favoring states' rights and agriculture — despite the Constitution not mentioning parties and Washington actively dreading them.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The First Party System lasted from roughly 1792 to 1824, when the Federalist Party effectively collapsed after backing the losing side in the War of 1812 and opposing westward expansion. Both parties began publishing rival newspapers to wage the fight: the Federalist Gazette of the United States versus the Democratic-Republican National Gazette, edited by poet Philip Freneau (whom Jefferson secretly put on the State Department payroll to attack Hamilton).

events.label: The French Revolution splits America
events.description: When France overthrew its king and went to war with monarchical Britain, Americans split hard along party lines — Democratic-Republicans cheered the sister republic, Federalists saw bloody anarchy — turning foreign policy into a domestic civil war before a single American shot was fired.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Revolution that began with the 1789 Estates General ended in November 1799 with Napoleon's coup — ten years of upheaval. Many of the Revolution's ideas are now considered foundational principles of liberal democracy; its values remain central to French political culture today. American enthusiasm began cooling sharply after 1793, when the guillotine took Louis XVI and the Terror began killing thousands.

events.label: Citizen Genêt affair
events.description: France's minister Edmond-Charles Genêt arrived in 1793 and immediately started recruiting Americans into privateering operations and military expeditions against Britain and Spain — on American soil, appealing directly to the public over Washington's head.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Genêt's own government eventually turned on him: the Girondin faction that sent him was overthrown by the Jacobins, who demanded his extradition — almost certainly a death sentence. Washington chose to let him stay in America rather than hand him to the guillotine, and Genêt settled permanently in New York, married a governor's daughter, and became an American citizen. His mission was the first real test of whether a foreign power could exploit American partisan divisions to override the executive branch.

events.label: Proclamation of Neutrality
events.description: On April 22, 1793, Washington formally declared the United States neutral in the war between Revolutionary France and Britain, and threatened legal proceedings against any American who aided either side — establishing that the president, not Congress, leads in foreign policy.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Nothing in the Constitution explicitly authorized the president to unilaterally declare national neutrality — the power was implied, not stated, and was immediately contested. The proclamation's constitutional logic was argued out in a famous newspaper pamphlet war between Hamilton (writing as 'Pacificus') and Madison (writing as 'Helvidius'), one of the first great constitutional debates about executive power. The text threatened criminal prosecution of any American who violated neutrality, a serious warning that carried real legal teeth.

events.label: Jay's Treaty
events.description: Jay's Treaty (1794) was a deal with Britain negotiated by Chief Justice John Jay that got British troops off American soil and averted a war the young republic couldn't afford — but outraged France and split American politics down the middle.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Jay was burned in effigy across the country when the treaty's terms became public; one pamphleteer wrote that he could travel from Boston to Philadelphia by the light of Jay burning in effigy along the road. The treaty said nothing about the British practice of impressment (seizing American sailors and forcing them into the Royal Navy), which was the loudest grievance. It did, however, open the British West Indies to American trade — one genuinely useful concession that got little credit at the time.

events.label: Pinckney's Treaty
events.description: Signed with a distracted, declining Spain in 1795, Pinckney's Treaty fixed the U.S. southern boundary at the 31st parallel and secured free navigation of the Mississippi River through Spanish New Orleans — the economic lifeline of every farmer west of the Appalachians.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The treaty also granted Americans the 'right of deposit' at New Orleans: the ability to store goods there duty-free while awaiting ocean-going ships, which was essential because bulky farm products couldn't be carried overland to Atlantic ports. Spain conceded so much partly because it feared the United States and Britain were about to ally against it after Jay's Treaty. When Spain briefly revoked the deposit right in 1802, it nearly triggered a war and was a direct driver of the Louisiana Purchase negotiations the following year.

events.label: Washington's Farewell Address
events.description: Washington's 1796 Farewell Address was never spoken aloud — it was published in a Philadelphia newspaper and reprinted nationwide as an open letter, a founding document warning against partisan 'spirit of party' and 'permanent alliances' with Europe's warring powers.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Hamilton drafted large sections of the address, working from an earlier Madison-drafted version Washington had shelved in 1792 when he first considered retiring. For much of the 19th century the address was read aloud in the U.S. Senate annually on Washington's birthday; the Senate still holds that reading every February. The 'permanent alliances' warning was eventually used to justify American reluctance to join the League of Nations in 1919 — one man's farewell shaping debates 123 years later.

events.label: Democratic-Republican Party forms
events.description: Thomas Jefferson and James Madison built the Democratic-Republican Party in the early 1790s around states' rights, agrarian economics, sympathy with Revolutionary France, and suspicion of concentrated federal power — the first organized opposition party in American history.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The party called itself simply 'the Republican Party' at the time; the 'Democratic-Republican' label is largely a historian's convention to avoid confusion with the later, unrelated Republican Party founded in 1854. It became the dominant party after 1800 as the Federalists collapsed, eventually splitting in the 1820s into the Democratic Party and the short-lived National Republicans. The tricolor cockade — the red, white, and blue rosette of the French Revolution — became a symbol that Democratic-Republicans wore to signal their sympathies.

events.label: Quasi-War with France
events.description: The Quasi-War (1798–1800) was an undeclared naval conflict between the United States and France, fought mostly in the Caribbean after France began seizing American merchant ships to retaliate for Jay's Treaty with Britain.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The U.S. Navy captured or recaptured over 80 French vessels during the conflict. The war produced one of the Navy's most celebrated early engagements: USS Constellation's defeat of the French frigate L'Insurgente in February 1799, one of the first major American naval victories. The conflict was ended not by battlefield loss but by diplomacy — Adams's peace mission to Paris in 1799.

events.label: XYZ Affair
events.description: When Adams sent a diplomatic commission to Paris in 1797, French agents (labeled X, Y, and Z in the published dispatches) demanded a large bribe just to begin talks — a humiliation that detonated American public opinion and nearly launched a full war.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The three French intermediaries had real identities: X was Jean-Conrad Hottinguer, Y was Pierre Bellamy, and Z was Lucien Hauteval, all working on behalf of foreign minister Talleyrand. The slogan 'Millions for defense, but not one cent for tribute' was actually coined by South Carolina congressman Robert Goodloe Harper, not by Adams himself. The affair's exposure was a political gift to the Federalists, who swept the 1798 midterm elections while the country seething with anti-French fury.

events.label: Naturalization Act of 1798
events.description: The Naturalization Act of 1798 tripled the residency period for citizenship — from five years to fourteen — targeting the wave of immigrants, particularly Irish and French, who were voting heavily Republican.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The law also extended the required 'Declaration of Intention' (the first step toward citizenship) from three years to five. It was one of four laws passed together as the Alien and Sedition Acts package; Congress repealed this one in 1802 under Jefferson, reverting the residency requirement to five years. The act never actually blocked large numbers of naturalizations; its primary effect was political intimidation.

events.label: The Sedition Act
events.description: The Sedition Act of 1798 made it a federal crime to publish 'false, scandalous, and malicious' criticism of the government — and it was enforced almost entirely against Republican editors and politicians who criticized President Adams.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: At least 25 people were arrested and 10 convicted under the act, including Matthew Lyon, a Republican congressman from Vermont, who was jailed for four months for writing a letter criticizing Adams's 'unbounded thirst for ridiculous pomp.' Remarkably, Lyon was re-elected to Congress from his jail cell. The act expired on its own terms on March 3, 1801 — the day before Jefferson's inauguration — and Jefferson pardoned all those convicted under it.

events.label: Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions
